chunks: "Frequency pulls efficiency and ripple in opposite directions.

Higher frequency lowers ripple and lets you use smaller inductors and capacitors, because the inductor ripple current is V out(1-D) over (Lf) and the capacitor ripple goes as 1 over f again on top of that.
But every switching event costs energy, so overlap loss, C oss loss, gate-drive loss, dead-time and recovery loss all scale with frequency.
How that plays out depends on what I hold fixed.

If I keep the same inductor, higher frequency reduces ripple current, which cuts RMS current and core loss, so efficiency actually improves a bit at first and then falls when switching loss takes over: in my 12 volts to 3.
3 volts, 2 amps example it peaks near 300 kilohertz at about 94% and drops to 92% at 1 megahertz and 80% at 5 megahertz.
If I instead shrink the inductor in proportion, to keep the same ripple current, then efficiency falls monotonically: 95. 5% at 100 kilohertz, 93.
5% at 500 kilohertz, 91% at 1 megahertz, but the inductor goes from 23 microhenries to 2. 4 microhenries.
So the choice is size and cost versus efficiency, and in practice it is bounded by EMI, minimum on-time and the control loop.
Typical point-of-load converters sit at 300 kilohertz to 2 megahertz."
